narrative:
The model predicted a 72.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3, compared with an average around the middle of the class (roughly 6th and 5.8th deciles) among accepted students, signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that is strongly associated with bar exam difficulty.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.5 it is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, which gave the model some reason to expect you might pass. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

The model did not consider your gender or race in any way. Your LSAT score of 38, family income in the upper-middle bracket, and plan to attend full-time were all close to or better than typical accepted students, yet they carried less weight in the final prediction.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and seeking targeted bar exam preparation resources before reapplying. Raising your class standing in future coursework would likely have the biggest positive effect on similar models. (218 words)
